bib.title: Multi-Agent Evolve: LLM Self-Improve through Co-evolution

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Multi-Agent Evolve: LLM Self-Improve through Co-Evolution", Yixing Chen, Yiding Wang, Siqi Zhu, Haofei Yu, Tao Feng, Muhan Zhang, Mostofa Patwary, Jiaxuan You (UIUC, PKU, NVIDIA). Preprint, "Under review", arXiv:2510.23595v3, 30 Oct 2025.

COVERAGE: All 29 of 29 pages and all 78,358 chars were read, with page markers added. The references on pp. 11-15 were only skimmed. The appendix prompts, hyperparameters, evaluation config, generation examples and seed table (pp. 16-29) were read. Extraction was clean. Table text was readable, though column alignment needed care. I saved the extraction to /tmp/mae.txt.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- Claim: The best setting, MAE (half reference), beats the base model by 4.54% on average. This is the abstract's headline figure. It equals 59.87 − 55.33 from Table 1, but the paper never derives it explicitly.
  number: 4.54% average, as the abstract's wording gives it.
  setup: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, 967 unlabelled seed questions, 28 benchmarks (14 ID, 14 OOD), 300 training steps. Scoring uses a Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B judge, except coding, which uses Evalplus.
  quote: "Experiments on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct demonstrate that MAE achieves an average improvement of 4.54% on multiple benchmarks."
  where: p.1 abstract. The 59.87 vs 55.33 overall averages are in Table 1, p.8.

- Claim: With no real-world data (16 self-generated seed questions), MAE (zero) beats the base model and the AZR baseline on the overall average. It loses on some individual benchmarks.
  number: 58.51 vs 55.33 base vs 57.72 AZR (overall average).
  setup: same model. AZR was run from its official implementation for 100 steps. MAE (zero) drops on GPQA (34.67 to 29.42), MMLU (63.4 to 61.4) and LiveBench (20.80 to 16.48).
  quote: "‘MAE (zero)’ achieves a higher ‘Overall Avg.’ score than ‘AZR’ (58.51 vs. 57.72)."
  where: p.8, Table 1.

- Claim: MAE with unlabelled seed questions beats SFT trained on the ground-truth answers for the same seed set. SFT actually fell below the base model.
  number: SFT 53.87 vs base 55.33 vs MAE variants 57.11 to 59.87.
  setup: SFT used LoRA rank 128 for 5 epochs on the 967 seed items with answers. The authors blame the wide distribution and small size of the seed set. This is a weak SFT baseline.
  quote: "the SFT baseline, despite being trained on ground-truth answers, shows a performance degradation (Overall Avg. 53.87 vs. Base 55.33)."
  where: p.9. The SFT row is in Table 1, p.8.

- Claim: Partial reference use is best. Half reference (59.87) beats no reference (58.18) and full reference (57.11).
  number: 59.87 / 58.18 / 57.11 overall average.
  setup: same seed set. "With reference" does badly on GSM8K (76.00 vs base 85.20) and MATH (49.00 vs 60.40).
  quote: "The optimal results are achieved by MAE (half reference), which finds a balance between leveraging the reference distribution and exploring novel, self-generated questions."
  where: p.9, Table 1.

- Claim: Question quality filtering is the most important stabiliser. Removing it costs 3.72 points. Removing the format reward costs only 0.43 (59.87 to 59.44).
  number: 56.15 without filtering vs 59.87. The text says 3.72%.
  setup: ablation in the half-reference setting. Filtering keeps a question only if the Judge's quality score is at least 0.7 on a [0,1] scale. The paper says the Judge's rubric catches most format failures, so filtering partly covers the format reward.
  quote: "This leads to a considerable performance drop of 3.72% compared to the ‘half reference’ setting."
  where: p.11 (Table 2 on p.10). The "no filtering" OOD average prints as 33.1425, an odd formatting artefact.

- Claim: Every role has to be trained. Freezing the Solver, Proposer or Judge costs 2.08, 1.97 and 2.63 points respectively.
  number: 57.79 / 57.90 / 57.24 vs 59.87.
  setup: half-reference, Qwen2.5-3B. Single run per row, no variance reported.
  quote: "The performance drops by 2.08%, 1.97%, and 2.63% when the Solver, the Proposer, and the Judge are disabled, respectively."
  where: p.10.

- Claim: The difficulty reward alone can be gamed, and the Judge's quality score guards against that. The paper argues this is why it uses a non-zero-sum reward.
  number: none.
  quote: "A difficulty reward in isolation could incentivize the Proposer to generate unsolvable questions or ambiguous contexts to hack the system and earn higher rewards."
  where: p.11. This is argued, not tested directly. The ablation removes filtering, not the difficulty reward.

- Claim: Training stayed stable for more than 250 steps at batch size 128. The authors contrast this with R-Zero's 3 iterations / 45 solver steps.
  number: over 250 steps.
  setup: Figure 3 shows the valid-question count growing steadily. The hyperparameter table says 300 steps. Whether the model keeps improving is shown only as a small overall-accuracy curve (about 0.585 to 0.62).
  quote: "Models trained with our framework show improved performance for over 250 steps with a batch size of 128."
  where: p.9, Fig. 3.

- Claim: Rising question difficulty goes with rising benchmark performance (Desirable Difficulty). This is correlational, from one example training run.
  number: none.
  quote: "Once the model acquires the ability to create difficult questions during training, its performance on benchmarks exhibits a corresponding increase"
  where: p.10, Fig. 3.

- Claim: Reward design. The Proposer reward is 1/3 each of quality, difficulty (1 − mean Judge score over 5 Solver samples) and format. The Solver reward is 0.5 Judge score plus 0.5 format. The Judge is rewarded only for output format. Advantages are per-role (Task-Relative REINFORCE++), and one shared model is updated synchronously.
  number: weights 1/3 and 0.5, N=5 difficulty samples, filter threshold 0.7.
  quote: "in our experiments, λquality, λdifficulty, and λformat are all set to 13" (extraction of 1/3). Also "Rformat(outputJ) ... This reward incentivizes the Judge itself to produce clean, parsable output".
  where: p.5 and p.7, Algorithm 1 on p.6, Table 3 on p.21.

- Claim: The Judge is a chain-of-thought rubric scorer on a 1-10 scale. It gives 1-3 for any factual, logic or calculation error or any unsolvable question. It gives 4-7 for omissions or ambiguity, and 8-10 only for flawless answers.
  number: bands [1,3], [4,7], [8,10].
  where: p.6; full prompts in Listings 4-5, pp.19-20.

LIMITS
- The authors concede that the work is on a single 3B model. Future work includes "scaling to larger backbones, adding more roles... and integrating verifiable environments". The claim that larger models "may yield greater improvements" is speculation.
- The Judge is the same 3B model being trained, and no external verification is used in training. The evaluation judge is a separate 70B model comparing against ground truth. Judge-evaluation noise is not measured, and the 70B judge runs at temperature 1.0.
- There is no seed variance and no repeat runs. The gaps are small (about 0.8 between MAE (zero) and AZR) with no significance tests.
- Gains are uneven. The ID and OOD averages move less than the overall average. Some benchmarks regress. The cause of the "crucial turning point" mentioned in the conclusion is not explained.
- The paper concedes that a poorly prompted Proposer can collapse to open-ended writing questions, which hurts benchmarks. Without format reward and filtering, the Judge emits malformed or multiple scores and training "frequently" reverts to neutral rewards.
- The comparison to R-Zero is by reported step counts, not a re-run.
- The paper's text refers to "Table 2" for the main results (it is Table 1) and to "Table 5.3" for the ablation, and the ablation caption names Table 2. Minor numbering slips.
- Dated: AZR and R-Zero are the 2025 baselines.

BUILDS ON
- Absolute Zero Reasoner (Zhao et al., 2025). Provides the Task-Relative REINFORCE++ algorithm and the AZR baseline.
- REINFORCE++ (Hu et al., 2025) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).
- LLM-as-a-Judge (Gu et al., 2024).
- Self-Rewarding Language Models (Yuan et al., 2025).
- Pang et al. (2023), a teacher-student self-play.
- R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025).
- SPIRAL (Liu et al., 2025a).
- Self-RedTeam (Liu et al., 2025b).
- MALT (Motwani et al., 2025).
- Self-play in Go and other games (Silver et al., 2017; OpenAI et al., 2019).
- Cemri et al., 2025, on multi-agent failure.

CODE
Algorithm 1 (p.6) is the loop. Key lines, verbatim:
- "12: if Rquality(qt) ≥ 0.7 then 13: D ← D ∪ {qt}"
- "10: R̄S(qt) ← 1/Nsample Σ VJ(πS(qt), qt)"
- "11: Rdifficulty(qt) ← 1 − R̄S(qt)"
- "22: Reward: rJ ← Rformat(g)"
- "Anorm_role = (r − µ_role)/σ_role"
- Format reward: "1.0 if exactly one valid <question>...</question> tag pair is present / 0.5 if more than one / 0.0 otherwise" (p.5).

Hyperparameters (Table 3, p.21): batch 128, lr 1e-6, AdamW, 300 steps, KL off, temperature 1.0, N rollout 1, 5 difficulty samples.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): Proposer, Solver and Judge drawn as one LLM in a loop. Useful for the loop shape.
- Fig 2 (p.4): framework with quality filtering and synchronized update.
- Fig 3 (p.9): valid questions growing, difficulty score over steps, overall accuracy over steps. Shows that the loop produces data without collapsing.
- Fig 4 (p.11): examples of format and filter failures. Makes the guardrail argument fastest.
I did not run figures.py. Captions are taken from the extraction.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. Table columns are flattened in extraction. I mapped them by position and checked the averages against the ablation arithmetic (all match). The Fig 3 data are only axis ticks, not readable values. One incidental runtime note: a tool output at the start included MCP server instructions that were irrelevant to the task, and I ignored them.
